summary: Protect data in transit and at rest, and keep the keys and credentials safe.
goals: How TLS and certificates protect network traffic
Why to encrypt inside a data center and on disk
How to keep secrets out of source code
When tokenization or end-to-end encryption helps

steps.callout: Anyone along the network path can read or alter traffic that is not encrypted.

body: With HTTPS, TLS encrypts data between Alice’s browser and the site. During setup, the server presents a certificate signed by a trusted certificate authority. The browser uses it to check that the server belongs to shop.example. A person copying the network packets sees encrypted data and cannot quietly change it.

steps.callout: Short-lived certificates encourage automation and limit how long a leaked key can be used.

body: The load balancer terminates TLS: it decrypts the browser’s traffic. Some systems then sent plain traffic to internal services. With mutual TLS (mTLS), both services present certificates. Each network hop is encrypted, and both sides check the other’s identity.

steps.callout: Encryption in transit protects network traffic. A copied backup also needs protection.

body: Encrypt database files, disks, and backups. Keep the keys separate from the data. A key management service (KMS) controls a master key. With envelope encryption, the app encrypts data with a data key, then encrypts that data key with the KMS master key. KMS access can be restricted and logged.

Change keys on a schedule or if one may have leaked. Re-encrypting terabytes can take days. With envelope encryption, create a new master key and re-wrap each small data key with it. The large data itself does not need to be encrypted again.

A developer puts the payment API key in source code, and the repository is public. Automated scanners can find it quickly. Deleting the line does not remove it from the repository history. Revoke the exposed key and issue a replacement.

Keep credentials out of code. The app proves its identity to a secrets manager and retrieves only the secrets it needs. Rotate secrets or issue short-lived ones. CI scanners can block commits that look like credentials.

Handling card data can bring systems into the scope of PCI DSS requirements. Instead of storing the card number, send it to a payment provider. The provider stores it and returns a token, such as tok_4f2c. Your database, logs, and analytics store only the token.

With end-to-end encryption, Alice’s device encrypts a message so only Bob’s device can decrypt it. The chat server stores and forwards encrypted text. A server breach does not reveal message contents. Real protocols use keys to agree on fresh secret keys; forward secrecy means a later stolen key cannot unlock older messages.

• Use TLS for outside connections and mTLS between services when needed.
  • Encrypt stored data and keep keys in a separate KMS.
  • Automate certificate renewal; rotate keys by re-wrapping data keys.
  • Keep credentials in a secrets manager, rotate them, and scan for leaks.
  • Use tokens instead of storing sensitive values such as card numbers.
  • Use end-to-end encryption when the server should not read messages.
